author: Platform Documentation
deck: The render service carries binary image bytes into a PDF through a dedicated asset channel, on both the chromium and typst renderers. Here is the supported path, how to verify it, and a correction to earlier guidance.
description: An operational runbook for embedding a real image in a generated PDF: the supported asset channel, the safe sequence for both chromium and typst, how to verify byte fidelity, and what to do when an image comes back wrong.

editorial.writer_notes: Documents session-11 testing: chromium image-embedding data-URI corruption threshold (safe below ~172 base64 chars, corrupted at 292+) and the first proven typst validate-publish-render cycle (text only; image embedding not yet supported).

public.body:
Two things needed proving on the render service: embedding a real, non-CSS image inside a generated PDF, and running the typst renderer end to end.

Both now work, on both engines, through one supported mechanism. This runbook documents that mechanism, the sequence to follow, and how to verify the result.

It also corrects an earlier version of this page. That version described a different, unsupported approach and reported a severe size limit for it. The limit was real for that approach, but the approach itself was the wrong one, and the guidance drawn from it was wrong. The correction is at the end.
public.title: Why this runbook exists

public.body:
Binary image bytes do not travel in the template. A published template holds layout only -- Liquid HTML and CSS for chromium, typst source for typst -- and neither carries an images field.

The bytes travel with the render job instead, in its assets payload. Every artifact job accepts an assets object alongside its data payload, of the form assets.images, where each entry names itself with an assetId.

Each entry supplies its bytes one of three ways: an inline dataUri, a blobKey pointing at a stored artifact, or a full artifactReference. Referencing a stored artifact is the one to prefer, because the bytes are resolved server-side and never pass through the caller at all.

The render service then makes those bytes available to the template under the assetId, and each engine reads them its own way:

On chromium, the asset is served from a virtual origin that exists only for the life of the render. The template references it as an ordinary image source at render.assets.invalid, followed by the assetId.

On typst, the asset is written into the render sandbox and loaded by path, as image of assets slash the assetId.

The network is otherwise closed. That virtual origin is one of only two hosts the renderer will serve, which is why this channel works while an ordinary remote image URL does not.
public.title: Prerequisites

public.body:
1. Create or locate the image artifact. A generated or imported image already stored against the article gives you a blobKey and a verified public path.

2. Author the template to reference the asset by name -- the virtual origin plus the assetId on chromium, or the assets path on typst. Do not add an images field to the template itself; only Liquid partials are recognised there.

3. Validate the template and poll until the report reaches a terminal PASSED state. The validation render has no assets attached, so the image will be absent from that proof -- an absent image does not fail validation, and should not be read as one.

4. Publish the template version. Chromium and typst both refuse to publish without a PASSED report for that exact version.

5. Create the render job with both payloads: data for the text bindings, assets.images for the bytes.

6. Verify the output before you rely on it.
public.title: Safe sequence

public.body:
A completed job reporting verified does not tell you the image inside the document is correct. Verification confirms the artifact was stored and is retrievable; it says nothing about what the renderer painted.

Check two things.

First, the output size. A render carrying a real image is dramatically larger than the same template without one. The reference render for this page went from about 13 KB at validation, with no asset attached, to about 632 KB once a 64 KB image was supplied. A render that did not grow did not embed anything.

Second, the pixels. Extract the embedded raster from the finished PDF and compare it against the source file directly, rather than looking at a preview. A partially decoded image is entirely capable of looking plausible at a glance and being wrong in its lower half.

That second check is not hypothetical. It is what caught the failure described in the correction below, and it is the only reason that failure was noticed at all.
public.title: Verification

public.body:
The image is missing entirely. The template's asset name and the job's assetId must match exactly. A mismatch is silent: the request for the missing name is refused by the closed network, the page renders without it, and the job still succeeds.

The image is present but visibly wrong -- truncated, or correct at the top and dark below. Stop using it and re-render through the asset channel. Do not compensate by shrinking the image.

The image bytes are rejected before rendering. The service decodes and checks image bytes before dispatching them, so a corrupt or truncated source fails fast and names the offending asset rather than producing a damaged document.

The render is larger than expected. Images are embedded at their natural resolution regardless of the size they are displayed at. Resize the source rather than scaling it down in CSS.

One standing rule underneath all of these: never embed an image by pasting base64 into a template binding. That path is not the supported channel, and it is where the failure below came from.
public.title: Failure recovery

public.body:
An earlier version of this page described embedding images by substituting a base64 data URI into a chromium template's HTML through its data payload, and reported that the result corrupted above roughly 172 base64 characters -- concluding that images had to be kept smaller than a postage stamp.

The corruption was real and is still reproducible in the affected documents: the lower two thirds of the test image is black in the stored PDF, and the source file it was built from is byte-identical to what was sent. That part of the earlier report stands.

The conclusion drawn from it did not. Data-URI substitution is not the supported mechanism for embedding an image, and the limit it appeared to impose is not a property of the renderer. The asset channel described above carries a 64 KB image through the same engine, in the same document, with no difficulty -- several hundred times past the ceiling the earlier guidance described.

The same correction applies to typst, which the earlier version reported as having no image support at all. It does, by the same asset channel.

The data-URI defect remains open and is worth fixing on its own merits, because it fails silently. It does not, however, constrain what any template can do today.
public.title: Correction to earlier guidance

public.body:
Two documents were produced while writing this runbook. The first is a one-page chromium render carrying a real 64 KB image through the asset channel: about 13 KB at validation with no asset attached, about 632 KB once the image was supplied. The second is a typst render of the same pipeline, with page geometry, colour and text all produced by typst's own layout engine.

Both are stored against this article. Download links are not attached yet: the publish gate checks a request-scoped artifact index that does not yet list them, and linking an artifact it cannot see would block this correction from shipping. The links will be added once that index resolves.

public.body: This runbook's typst proof: the first complete validate-publish-render cycle run on the typst renderer for this deployment, producing a correct one-page PDF from the template's own layout engine.
